deed: לודוויק הירשפלד שותף לגילוי תורשת סוגי הדם וארגן חיסונים בגטו ורשה
title: Ludwik Hirszfeld showed that blood groups are inherited, and in the Warsaw Ghetto he secretly vaccinated against typhus

trailer.text: Ludwik Hirszfeld was a Polish Jewish microbiologist and serologist, and together with Emil von Dungern he gave the blood groups the names A, B and O, which have been used since.
The two showed that blood groups are heritable traits.
In February 1941 he and his wife were forced to move to the Warsaw Ghetto, and there he headed the Health Council.
There he and his colleagues secretly vaccinated people against typhus, and despite a severe shortage of medications and disinfectants he managed to improve the health conditions.
After the war, together with the obstetrician Kazimierz Jabłoński, he introduced exchange transfusion as a treatment for fetuses and newborns, and this therapy saved the lives of almost 200 children.

glance.label: The discovery
glance.value: Inherited blood groups, the names A, B, O

glance.label: Recognition
glance.value: Nominated for the Nobel Prize in 1950

stations.title: A child of a Jewish family

paragraphs.text: Ludwik Hirszfeld was born in 1884 into a Jewish family.
According to Mayo Clinic Proceedings, he was the son of a rich industrialist.
According to Wikipedia and Encyclopedia.com, he studied medicine in Germany.
According to an article in Acta Poloniae Historica, he and his wife converted to Catholicism, but in the eyes of the Germans this changed nothing.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, Hirszfeld was born in Warsaw.
Hirszfeld and von Dungern examined 348 people from 72 families.
They showed that blood group A or B appears in a child only if it appeared in at least one of the parents.
In this way the two showed that blood groups are inherited, and established the terminology of the ABO system.
They gave the blood groups the names A, B and O, which have been used since.
A year later they showed that type A blood cells can clump together strongly or weakly, and proposed two subtypes: A1 and A2.
Karl Landsteiner said in his Nobel lecture that the principal results in the study of the hereditary transmission of blood groups were owed to the work of von Dungern and Hirszfeld.
In Serbia, Hirszfeld, his wife and Serbian medical personnel tried to stop the typhus epidemic through mass disinfection.
According to the review, the epidemic was eventually stopped, but the death toll was enormous: about 300,000 Serbian civilians and 100,000 soldiers.
There Hirszfeld also isolated two new strains that cause paratyphoid fever, and one of them was later named Salmonella hirszfeldii.
He nearly died after ordering that he be given too high a dose of quinine for malaria.
According to BioBridge Global, during the war he and his wife collected blood samples from thousands of soldiers of different peoples.
Hirszfeld and his wife Hanna tested more than 8,000 people from at least 16 groups, and found that the frequency of each blood group differed from one people to another.
According to Wikipedia, their report was published in The Lancet in 1919, and was the first paper to show this difference between populations.
In independent Poland, with the support of Ludwik Rajchman, Hirszfeld assumed responsibility for establishing an institute for serum research.
This institute later became the National Institute of Hygiene.
He organized blood donation centers, and thanks to him Poland was the first country in Europe to regulate the matter of blood donors by law.
It seems that he was the first to propose that blood incompatibility between mother and fetus may cause miscarriage or disease of the fetus or newborn.
During the siege of Warsaw in 1939 he was urged to flee, but he chose to stay and organize a blood transfusion camp for the soldiers.
The Institute of Blood Transfusion was destroyed in one of the first German air raids, so he organized blood transfusions at the Ujazdowski Hospital.
When the war broke out he was dismissed from the Institute of Hygiene because of his Jewish origin.
When the Germans ordered all Jews to wear a yellow armband, he ignored the order.
In the autumn of 1940 the Germans began forming a ghetto in Warsaw, crowding over 300,000 people into an area of 2.9 km².
Food rations were less than 400 calories a day, and there were almost no health services.
Every month, between 3,000 and 5,000 people died in the ghetto.
In February 1941 the Hirszfelds were forced to move to the ghetto.
Adam Czerniaków, chairman of the Jewish community in the ghetto, asked Hirszfeld to act against typhus, which, alongside hunger, was the main cause of death.
Hirszfeld headed the Health Council and did his best to slow down the epidemic.
He and his colleagues secretly vaccinated people with the vaccine of Prof. Rudolf Weigl from his institute in Lwów.
Later, Dr. Edmund Wojciechowski prepared the vaccine at the National Institute of Hygiene according to Weigl's protocol, and the vaccine was smuggled into the ghetto.
They also designed a simple test to detect typhus bacteria in urine.
Róża Amzel, his former assistant at the institute, also lived in the ghetto and helped him greatly; she was later murdered by the Nazis.
According to Wikipedia, the local priest Marceli Godlewski also helped him.
According to Wikipedia and the Forward, Hirszfeld held secret medical courses in the ghetto.
Over 500 students attended these courses, and fewer than 50 of them survived the war.
Before September 1942, over 300,000 Jews were deported from the Warsaw Ghetto to Treblinka.
The Hirszfelds managed to escape from the ghetto.
The dangerous and costly escape was organized by Konstanty Potocki, an apothecary who ran a pharmacy outside the ghetto.
Dr. Feliks Przesmycki, a former associate at the institute, provided them with forged documents.
According to Mayo Clinic Proceedings, they lived in secret in small villages in central Poland.
According to the 1943.pl website, Hirszfeld hid under an assumed name in the home of Laura Kenig in Stara Miłosna.
Their only daughter, Maria, died in the neighbouring village of Kocina and was buried in a small cemetery under a false name, Maria Halecka.
According to Archives of Hellenic Medicine, she died in 1943 at the age of 23.
After the war Hirszfeld, together with the obstetrician Kazimierz Jabłoński, introduced exchange transfusion as a treatment for hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.
This therapy saved the lives of almost 200 children.
In 1950 he was nominated for the Nobel Prize for explaining the blood conflict between mother and fetus.
He helped to organize the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Wrocław, and was its first dean.
He and his wife resisted pressure from the authorities and did not join the Communist Party, which was unusual among prominent scientists.
He wrote almost 400 works in German, French, English and Polish.
He received honorary doctorates from the University of Prague in 1950 and the University of Zurich in 1951.
Hirszfeld died on March 7, 1954 and was buried at the St. Laurentis cemetery in Wrocław.
Felix Milgrom wrote that Hirszfeld belongs to the extinct group of scientists who created the fields of immunohematology and immunogenetics.
In 2009 the Polish Post issued a stamp bearing his image.
According to the Polish Academy of Sciences (PAN), the Ludwik Hirszfeld Institute of Immunology and Experimental Therapy in Wrocław was founded in 1952.
According to the review in Vox Sanguinis, it may be argued that Hirszfeld's theory of "races" by blood group reinforced the idea of a hierarchy among races, although he did not intend this.
His studies on the frequency of blood groups sparked controversies with Soviet scientists who criticized them.
In the Gorgonowa case, the most popular trial in Poland between the two wars, Hirszfeld cast doubt on the experts' blood test, but Gorgonowa was found guilty.
According to Hektoen International, because he was born to a Jewish family, he faced obstacles in occupied Poland in publishing his work and in remaining a lecturer.

claims.text: לפי אתר 1943.pl, אחרי הבריחה הסתתר הירשפלד תחת שם בדוי בביתה של לאורה קניג בסטרה מיווסנה.
claims.quote: he hid under an assumed name in the home of Laura Kenig in Stara Miłosna near Warsaw

claims.text: בתם היחידה מריה מתה בכפר קוצ'ינה ונקברה בבית קברות קטן בשם בדוי, מריה האלצקה.
claims.quote: Their only daughter Maria died in the neighbouring village of Kocina and was buried at a small cemetery under the false name of Maria Halecka.

claims.text: לפי מאמר ב-Archives of Hellenic Medicine, לזוג הייתה בת אחת, שמתה ב-1943 בגיל 23.
claims.quote: The Hirszfelds had one daughter, who died in 1943 at the age of 23.

claims.text: הירשפלד סייע בארגון הפקולטה לרפואה באוניברסיטת ורוצלב והיה הדיקן הראשון שלה.
claims.quote: Ludwik Hirszfeld helped to organize the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Wrocław, and became its first dean.

claims.text: שני בני הזוג הירשפלד עמדו בלחץ הרשויות ולא הצטרפו למפלגה הקומוניסטית, דבר חריג בקרב מדענים בולטים.
claims.quote: Both Hirszfelds resisted the pressure from the officials and never joined the Communist party, which was unusual at the time

claims.text: הירשפלד כתב כמעט 400 עבודות בגרמנית, צרפתית, אנגלית ופולנית.
claims.quote: He wrote almost 400 works in German, French, English, and Polish

claims.text: הירשפלד קיבל תארי דוקטור לשם כבוד מאוניברסיטאות פראג (1950) וציריך (1951).
claims.quote: Hirszfeld received many honors, including honorary doctorates from the universities of Prague (1950) and Zurich (1951).

claims.text: הירשפלד מת ב-7 במרץ 1954 ונקבר בבית הקברות סנט לורנס בוורוצלב.
claims.quote: He died on March 7th, 1954 and was buried at the St. Laurentis cemetery in Wrocław.

claims.text: פליקס מילגרום כתב שהירשפלד שייך לקבוצה שנכחדה של מדענים שיצרו את תחומי האימונוהמטולוגיה והאימונוגנטיקה.
claims.quote: Hirszfeld belongs to the extinct group of scientists who created the fields of immunohematology and immunogenetics.

claims.text: הדואר הפולני הנפיק בול עם דמותו של הירשפלד ב-2009.
claims.quote: The Polish Post issued a stamp with Ludwik Hirszfeld in 2009

claims.text: לפי הסקירה, ניתן לטעון שתיאוריית הגזעים הסרולוגיים של הירשפלד חיזקה את ההיררכיה הגזעית, אף שלא היה זה בכוונתו.
claims.quote: So, it may be argued that Hirszfeld's theory of serological races buttressed the racial hierarchy, although it was not his intent to reinforce

claims.text: מחקריו על שכיחות סוגי הדם עוררו מחלוקות עם מדענים סובייטים מבקרים.
claims.quote: His studies on the frequency of ABO blood groups also sparked controversies with visiting Soviet scientists

claims.text: בפרשת גורגונובה, המשפט הפופולרי ביותר בפולין בין המלחמות, הטיל הירשפלד ספק בבדיקת הדם של המומחים, אך גורגונובה נמצאה אשמה.
claims.quote: Eventually, however, Gorgonowa was found guilty and sentenced to prison.

claims.text: לפי Hektoen International, בהיותו יליד משפחה יהודית נתקל הירשפלד במכשולים בפרסום עבודותיו ובהמשך עבודתו כמרצה בפולין הכבושה.
claims.quote: Having been born to a Jewish family, he faced obstacles in both publishing his work and remaining a lecturer in occupied Poland.

claims.text: לפי מרכז הרפואי של אוניברסיטת קנזס, הירשפלד התנצר בהיידלברג.
claims.quote: While in Heidelberg Ludwik became a Catholic, he

claims.text: לפי BioBridge Global, הירשפלד ואשתו נמלטו מהגטו ב-1941.
claims.quote: He and Hanna escaped the ghetto in 1941.

claims.text: לפי אתר 1943.pl, הירשפלד נמלט מהגטו לצד הארי ביולי 1942.
claims.quote: In July 1942, he escaped from the ghetto to the Aryan side.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית (Encyclopaedia Judaica), הירשפלד נולד בוורשה.
claims.quote: Hirszfeld, who was born in Warsaw, spent from 1907 to 1911 in Heidelberg.

claims.text: לפי האקדמיה הפולנית למדעים (PAN), המכון לאימונולוגיה וטיפול ניסויי על שם לודוויק הירשפלד בוורוצלב נוסד ב-1952.
claims.quote: The Ludwik Hirszfeld Institute of Immunology and Experimental Therapy in Wrocław (IITD PAN) was founded in 1952.
